title: Hickson Compact Group 31: interacting galaxies glow with millions of young stars
caption: Hickson Compact Group 31, imaged by the Hubble, Spitzer and GALEX space telescopes
captureDate: Hubble data: 8 August 2006; Spitzer: 22 February 2005; GALEX: 27 December 2004

celestial: HCG 31, Hickson Compact Group 31 · constellation Eridanus · about 180 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, S. Gallagher (The University of Western Ontario) and J. English (University of Manitoba)

recognition.text: Published in the ESA/Hubble image archive. No published rating.

story: A bright, distorted object sits left of center in this composite, with a cigar-shaped galaxy above it, a bridge of star clusters linking them, and a long rope of bright clusters leading to another galaxy at lower right. The bright object in the middle is simply a foreground star. These are members of Hickson Compact Group 31, four dwarf galaxies about 166 million light-years away.

The distorted object is actually two dwarf galaxies colliding head-on. Myriad star clusters have formed in the debris pulled from them and at the site of the crash, and the massive, hot young stars are pouring out ultraviolet radiation that heats nearby gas clouds and makes them glow.
Encounters like this between dwarf galaxies are usually seen billions of light-years away, and so billions of years in the past. This group is unusually close, offering a nearer look at the process.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.25 x 3.03 arcminutes) and distance (180 million light years), the frame spans roughly 170,000 × 159,000 light-years. Its light set out about 180 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This composite combines visible and near-infrared light from Hubble's ACS and WFPC2 cameras, infrared from NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope, and ultraviolet from GALEX. The color assigned to each dataset is not published.

explore: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys resolved the youngest and brightest clusters, letting astronomers estimate their ages. The brightest, hefty groups of at least 100,000 stars apiece, are under 10 million years old.
The galaxies appear to be entering the final stages of assembly, and astronomers expect them to become one large elliptical galaxy in another billion years.
